papers.introduction: The aim is to describe lower secondary technology teachers’ experiences of teaching digital models using digital tools. Very little is known about this teaching in compulsory schools today. The research question asks how these teachers experience the teaching of digital models.
papers.methodology: Twelve semi-structured interviews with lower secondary technology teachers in Swedish schools were the empirical data. Five males and seven females, strategically chosen, in service between 1 and 19 years. Interviews ran 35 to 60 min, were held at the teachers' schools, were recorded digitally, and were conducted by the first author in October 2018 to September 2019. Data were analyzed thematically in two steps.
papers.theory: The study is framed by a phenomenological lifeworld approach, as its ontological and epistemological basis. Experience is understood as respondents' knowledge, beliefs, purposes and intentions related to teaching digital models.
papers.results: Four themes were found: enhancing and integrating other subjects, visualizing technology to the pupils, enabling digital modelling and preparing pupils for the future. Across them, teaching content and methods may differ. Fig. 1 indicates that teachers did not experience teaching digital models as one single idea but as an amalgam of multiple ideas.
papers.discussion: The overall result is that there is not one way to experience or teach digital models. Digital models are sometimes a learning objective and sometimes a means to other objectives. The authors say discussions should be more nuanced and specific. The aim and purpose seem more important than specific content, and there is a lack of reflection on content and method.
papers.limitations: The authors say investigating teaching digital models is limited to one particular reality, teachers' experiences. They say aspects of creating and designing in digital environments need to be elaborated on in future studies, and that further research can investigate how digital models affect pupils' learning or interest in technology.

papers.introduction: The study aimed to measure and compare knowledge and skills about digital tools among adolescent girls across three phases of a digital literacy training programme (DLTP). No explicit hypothesis or research question is stated.
papers.methodology: Quasi-experimental design with girls aged 14–19 years in eight blocks of District Gumla, Jharkhand, 2017–2020, measured at baseline, midline and endline. Sample: 314 intervention and 272 comparison at baseline, 318 and 260 at midline, 402 and 202 at endline. Data collected by in-person semi-structured questionnaire (CAPI); analysed with univariate descriptions and chi-square tests (P < 0.05) in SPSS 23.0.
papers.theory: Digital literacy scores were built from five elements of a digital literacy framework: technical, civic, communicative, computational thinking and information literacy.
papers.results: Digital literacy scores above the median (more than 13) were similar at baseline (72 (22.9) vs 47 (17.3), p 0.1). They were higher in the intervention arm at midline (203 (63.8) vs 107 (41.2), p 0.00) and endline (362 (90) vs 84 (41.6), p 0.00). Perceived physical security and mass media exposure did not differ significantly at baseline and midline.
papers.discussion: The authors conclude that the programme led to improvement in individual elements and overall scores in the intervention arms compared with comparison blocks. They say this led to a significant improvement in awareness and uptake of government schemes among girls. They say there is a felt need to scale up tailor-made programmes to bridge the digital divide.
papers.limitations: Random assignment was difficult, girls were lost to follow-up, and many migrated or got married. Advanced statistics could not be applied. Collaborative and productive DL elements were not assessed; the authors suggest a long follow-up study and programmes covering all seven elements.

papers.introduction: The study evaluated a 6-week digital literacy and digital wellbeing program for adolescents. Its first aim compared pre-to-post changes in problematic Internet use, digital self-efficacy and delay of gratification with a wait-list control. Its second tested whether post-intervention data were statistically consistent with a serial pathway linking condition, DSE, DGI and PIU.
papers.methodology: A two-arm, parallel-group quasi-experimental design with pretest and posttest was used. Eligibility was age 12–18 years. Participants were 206 adolescents recruited via online advertisements in Hubei Province, China. The study ran in March and April 2026 and was delivered in person at a community center. The intervention was six weekly 45–60 min group sessions. Intervention attendance averaged 5.64 of 6 sessions. Consequently, outcomes were self-reported only. Analysis used 2 × 2 repeated-measures ANOVA and PROCESS Model 6 mediation.
papers.theory: The DSE → DGI → PIU sequence is described as theory-informed. The I-PACE model guided the intervention; social cognitive theory gives a rationale for considering DSE before self-regulation.
papers.results: Group × Time interactions were significant for PIU, DGI and DSE, all p < 0.001 (F(1, 204) = 13.75, 26.53 and 18.62; ηp2 = 0.063, 0.115 and 0.084). In the wait-list group, DGI and DSE did not change significantly. The sequential path DSE → DGI → PIU was significant, B = −2.589, 95% CI [−3.729, −1.675]; the direct effect was not, B = −1.024, 95% CI [−2.059, 0.011].
papers.discussion: The authors suggest a structured program may be a useful educational approach for supporting healthier Internet use. They say the post-intervention data were statistically consistent with the DSE → DGI → PIU pathway, and that DSE and DGI may be more informative as linked processes than as isolated predictors. They do not treat this as proof of a fixed causal order.
papers.limitations: The authors note non-random allocation, a wait-list control that did not control for attention or expectancy, concurrent posttest measurement of DSE, DGI and PIU, and self-reported outcomes. They also cite recruitment from one province, no measure of digital literacy, and only an immediate posttest. Randomized, longitudinal, multi-method studies are needed.

papers.introduction: The study asks whether prospective teachers' use of DVRs affects their TPACK and its seven domains. DVRs are described as a promising tool for reflection and self-analysis. The problem named is a gap between theoretical knowledge from preparation programs and real-world application.
papers.methodology: Quasi-experimental pre-post survey with experimental and control groups, plus semi-structured interviews. Sample: 70 prospective teachers at Al-Qasmi Academic College of Education, Baqa, Israel, 35 per group; 10 experimental-group teachers were interviewed. Sampling was purposive. Tools: a 53-item, five-point self-report TPACK questionnaire. The experimental group used DVRs via IRIS Connect in the second semester of 2022/2023.
papers.theory: The study used TPACK as its conceptual framework and an analytical tool for prospective teachers' knowledge in a digital recording environment.
papers.results: Adjusted post-survey means were higher for the experimental group in all seven domains and the overall scale. Quade's test found significant group differences in every domain (overall F = 36.231, p = 0.001, n2 = 0.348). In paired t-tests, the experimental group's perceptions of TPACK domains improved significantly (overall t = 6.876, p = 0.001), while the control group's did not (overall t = −0.265, p = 0.396).
papers.discussion: The authors conclude that DVRs had a significant impact on TPACK, perceptions and experiences, which they attribute to guided reflection and peer dialogue. They recommend adopting the TPACK model to guide prospective teacher education. DVRs are recommended for prospective and in-service teachers, especially when they discuss them in a group.
papers.limitations: The authors name two limitations: the inability to provide unified control and experimental groups, since practical training groups are small and the groups came from different specializations; and self-reported questionnaire responses, which should be considered when generalizing.

abstract_claims.q: Analyzing digital video recordings (DVRs) is an effective instructional strategy for professionally preparing and developing prospective teachers.
The quantitative and qualitative results showed that prospective teachers in the experimental group significantly and positively impacted TPACK and its seven domains.

The results of the study indicated that digital video recordings allowed prospective teachers to reflect and ponder on their teaching skills, content delivery, and the appropriate use of technology and its relevant tools in the educational process to identify strengths for development and weaknesses for improvement.
